{{Short description|Physics theorem for symmetries of action}}
[[File:Noether.jpg | thumb | right | alt=alt=Refer to caption | Portrait of Emmy Noether, around 1900.]]
In [[mathematics]] and [[theoretical physics]], '''Noether's second theorem''' relates symmetries of an [[action (physics)|action]] [[functional (mathematics)|functional]] with a system of [[differential equation]]s.<ref>{{Citation  |last=Noether  |first=Emmy  |year=1918  |title=Invariante Variationsprobleme  |url=https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/Invariante_Variationsprobleme  |journal=Nachr. D. König. Gesellsch. D. Wiss. Zu Göttingen, Math-phys. Klasse  |volume=1918  |pages=235–257 }}
:Translated in {{cite journal  |last1=Noether  |first1=Emmy  |year=1971  |title=Invariant variation problems |journal=[[Transport Theory and Statistical Physics]]  |volume=1  |issue=3  |pages=186–207  |arxiv=physics/0503066  |bibcode=1971TTSP....1..186N  |doi=10.1080/00411457108231446|s2cid=119019843 }}</ref> The theorem is named after its discoverer, [[Emmy Noether]].

The action ''S'' of a [[physical system]] is an [[integral]] of a so-called [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] function ''L'', from which the system's behavior can be determined by the [[principle of least action]]. Specifically, the theorem says that if the action has an infinite-dimensional [[Lie algebra]] of [[infinitesimal]] symmetries parameterized linearly by ''k'' arbitrary functions and their derivatives up to order ''m'', then the [[functional derivative]]s of ''L'' satisfy a system of ''k'' differential equations.

Noether's second theorem is sometimes used in [[gauge theory]].  Gauge theories are the basic elements of all modern [[field theory (physics)|field theories]] of physics, such as the prevailing [[Standard Model]].

== Mathematical formulation ==

=== First variation formula ===
Suppose that we have a [[dynamical system]] specified in terms of <math display="inline">m</math> independent variables <math display="inline">x=(x^1,\dots,x^m )</math>, <math display="inline">n</math> dependent variables <math display="inline">u=(u^1,\dots, u^n )</math>, and a [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] function <math display="inline">L(x,u,u_{(1)}\dots,u_{(r)})</math> of some finite order <math display="inline">r</math>. Here <math display="inline">u_{(k)}=(u^\sigma_{i_1...i_k})=(d_{i_1}\dots d_{i_k}u^\sigma)</math> is the collection of all <math display="inline">k</math>th order partial derivatives of the dependent variables. As a general rule, Latin indices <math display="inline">i,j,k,\dots</math> from the middle of the alphabet take the values <math display="inline">1,\dots,m</math>, Greek indices take the values <math display="inline">1,\dots,n</math>, and the [[Einstein notation|summation convention]] apply to them. Multiindex notation for the Latin indices is also introduced as follows. A ''multiindex'' <math display="inline">I</math> of length <math display="inline">k</math> is an ordered list <math>I=(i_1,\dots,i_k )</math> of <math display="inline">k</math> ordinary indices. The length is denoted as <math display="inline">\left|I \right|=k</math>. The summation convention does not directly apply to multiindices since the summation over lengths needs to be displayed explicitly, e.g. <math display="block">\sum_{|I|=0}^r f_I g^I = fg + f_i g^i + f_{ij} g^{ij} + \dots + f_{i_1...i_r} g^{i_1...i_r}.</math> The variation of the Lagrangian with respect to an arbitrary variation <math display="inline">\delta u^\sigma</math> of the dependent variables is <math display="block">\delta L = \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma} \delta u^\sigma + \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_i}\delta u ^\sigma_i 
+ \dots + \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_{i_1...i_r}} \delta u^\sigma_{i_1...i_r}
= \sum_{|I|=0}^r \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_I}\delta u^\sigma_I,</math> and applying the [[Integration by parts|inverse product rule of differentiation]] we get <math display="block">\delta L = E_\sigma \delta u^\sigma + d_i\left(\sum_{|I|=0}^{r-1} P^{iI}_\sigma
\delta u^\sigma_I\right),</math> where <math display="block">E_\sigma=\frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma} - d_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_i} +\dots
+ (-1)^r d_{i_1}\dots d_{i_r} \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_{i_1...i_r}}
= \sum_{|I|=0}^r (-1)^{|I|}d_I \frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_I}</math> are the [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler-Lagrange expressions]] of the Lagrangian, and the coefficients <math display="inline">P^I_\sigma</math> (Lagrangian momenta) are given by <math display="block">P^I_\sigma = \sum_{|J|=0}^{r-|I|}(-1)^{|J|}d_J\frac{\partial L}{\partial u^\sigma_{IJ}}.</math>

=== Variational symmetries ===
A variation <math display="inline">\delta u^\sigma = X^\sigma(x,u,u_{(1)},\dots)</math> is an ''infinitesimal symmetry'' of the Lagrangian <math display="inline">L</math> if <math display="inline">\delta L = 0</math> under this variation. It is an infinitesimal ''quasi-symmetry'' if there is a current <math display="inline">K^i=K^i(x,u,\dots)</math> such that <math display="inline">\delta L = d_i  K^i </math>.

It should be remarked that it is possible to extend infinitesimal (quasi-)symmetries by including variations with <math>\delta x^i \neq  0</math> as well, i.e. the independent variables are also varied. However such symmetries can always be rewritten so that they act only on the dependent variables. Therefore, in the sequel we restrict to so-called ''vertical variations'' where <math>\delta x^i = 0</math>.

For Noether's second theorem, we consider those variational symmetries (called ''[[Gauge symmetry (mathematics)|gauge symmetries]]'') which are parametrized linearly by a set of arbitrary functions and their derivatives. These variations have the generic form <math display="block">\delta_\lambda u^\sigma = R^\sigma_a \lambda^a + R^{\sigma,i}_{a}\lambda^a_{i} + \dots + R^{\sigma,i_1...i_s}_a \lambda^a_{i_1...i_s}
= \sum_{|I|=0}^s R^{\sigma,I}_a \lambda^a_I,</math>where the coefficients <math>R^{\sigma,I}_a</math> can depend on the independent and dependent variables as well as the derivatives of the latter up to some finite order, the <math>\lambda^a =  \lambda^a (x)</math> are arbitrarily specifiable functions of the independent variables, and the Latin indices <math>a,b,\dots</math> take the values <math>1,\dots,q</math>, where <math>q</math> is some positive integer.

For these variations to be (exact, i.e. not quasi-) gauge symmetries of the Lagrangian, it is necessary that <math>\delta_\lambda L = 0</math> for all possible choices of the functions <math>\lambda^a (x)</math>. If the variations are quasi-symmetries, it is then necessary that the current also depends linearly and differentially on the arbitrary functions, i.e. then <math>\delta_\lambda L =d_i K^i_\lambda</math>, where<math display="block">K^i_\lambda = K^i_a \lambda^a + K^{i,j}_a \lambda^a_{j} + K^{i,j_1j_2}_a \lambda^a_{j_1j_2}\dots</math>For simplicity, we will assume that all gauge symmetries are exact symmetries, but the general case is handled similarly.

=== Noether's second theorem ===
The statement of Noether's second theorem is that whenever given a Lagrangian <math display="inline">L</math> as above that admits gauge symmetries <math>\delta_\lambda u^\sigma </math> parametrized linearly by <math>q</math> arbitrary functions and their derivatives, then there exist <math>q</math> linear differential relations between the Euler-Lagrange equations of <math display="inline">L</math>.

Combining the first variation formula together with the fact that the variations <math display="inline">\delta_\lambda  u^\sigma </math> are symmetries, we get<math display="block">0 = E_\sigma \delta_\lambda u^\sigma + d_i W^i_\lambda,\quad
W^i_\lambda = \sum_{|I|=0}^r P^{iI}_\sigma  \delta_\lambda u^\sigma,</math>where on the first term proportional to the Euler-Lagrange expressions, further integrations by parts can be performed as<math display="block">E_\sigma \delta_\lambda u^\sigma = \sum_{|I|=0}^s E_\sigma R^{\sigma, I}_a \lambda^a_I
= Q_a\lambda^a + d_i\left(\sum_{|I|=0}^{s-1} Q^{iI}_a \lambda^a_I \right),</math>where<math display="block">Q^I_a = \sum_{|J|=0}^{s-|I|}(-1)^{|J|}d_J\left( E_\sigma R^{\sigma,IJ}_a \right),</math>in particular for <math display="inline">|I| = 0</math>,<math display="block">Q_a = E_\sigma R^\sigma_a - d_i\left( E_\sigma R^{\sigma,i}_a\right)+\dots +
(-1)^s d_{i_1}\dots d_{i_s}\left( E_\sigma R^{\sigma,i_1...i_s}_a \right)
= \sum_{|I|=0}^s (-1)^{|I|} d_I\left(E_\sigma R^{\sigma,I}_a\right) .</math>Hence, we have an ''[[On shell and off shell|off-shell]]'' relation <math display="block">0 = Q_a\lambda^a + d_i S^i_\lambda,</math>where <math display="inline">S^i_\lambda = H^i_\lambda + W^i_\lambda,</math> with <math display="inline">H^i_\lambda = \sum_{|I|=0}^{s-1} Q^{iI}_a\lambda^a_I</math>. This relation is valid for any choice of the gauge parameters <math display="inline">\lambda^a (x)</math>. Choosing them to be compactly supported, and integrating the relation over the manifold of independent variables, the integral total divergence terms vanishes due to [[Generalized Stokes theorem|Stokes' theorem]]. Then from the [[fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations]], we obtain that <math>Q_a\equiv 0</math> identically as ''off-shell'' relations (in fact, since the <math>Q_a</math> are linear in the Euler-Lagrange expressions, they necessarily vanish on-shell). Inserting this back into the initial equation, we also obtain the off-shell conservation law <math>d_i S^i_\lambda = 0</math>.

The expressions <math>Q_a</math> are differential in the Euler-Lagrange expressions, specifically we have<math display="block">Q_a = \mathcal D_a[E] = \sum_{|I|=0}^s (-1)^{|I|} d_I\left(E_\sigma R^{\sigma,I}_a\right)
= \sum_{|I|=0}^s F^{\sigma, I}_a d_I E_\sigma,</math>where<math display="block">F^{\sigma,I}_a = \sum_{|J|=0}^{s-|I|} \binom{|I|+|J|}{|I|} (-1)^{|I|+|J|} d_J R^{\sigma,IJ}_a.</math>Hence, the equations<math display="block">0 = \mathcal{D}_a[E]</math>are <math display="inline">q</math> differential relations to which the Euler-Lagrange expressions are subject to, and therefore the Euler-Lagrange equations of the system are not independent.

=== Converse result ===
A converse of the second Noether theorem can also be established. Specifically, suppose that the Euler-Lagrange expressions <math>E_\sigma</math> of the system are subject to <math>q</math> differential relations<math display="block">0 = \mathcal D_a[E] = \sum_{|I|=0}^s F^{\sigma,I}_a d_I E_\sigma.</math>Letting <math display="inline">\lambda = (\lambda^1,\dots,\lambda^q )</math> be an arbitrary <math display="inline">q</math>-[[tuple]] of functions, the [[Differential operator#Formal adjoint in one variable|formal adjoint]] of the operator <math display="inline">\mathcal{D}_a </math> acts on these functions through the formula<math display="block">E_\sigma (\mathcal{D}^+)^\sigma[\lambda] - \lambda^a\mathcal{D}_a [E] = d_i B^i_\lambda,</math>which defines the adjoint operator <math>(\mathcal{D}^+)^\sigma </math> uniquely. The coefficients of the adjoint operator are obtained through integration by parts as before, specifically<math display="block">(\mathcal{D}^+)^\sigma [\lambda] = \sum_{|I|=0}^s R^{\sigma,I}_a \lambda^a_I,</math>where<math display="block">R^{\sigma,I}_a = \sum_{|J|=0}^{s-|I|} (-1)^{|I|+|J|} \binom{|I|+|J|}{|I|} d_J F^{\sigma,IJ}_a.</math>Then the definition of the adjoint operator together with the relations <math>0 = \mathcal{D}_a [E]</math> state that for each <math display="inline">q</math>-tuple of functions <math>\lambda</math>, the value of the adjoint on the functions when contracted with the Euler-Lagrange expressions is a total divergence, viz. <math>E_\sigma(\mathcal{D}^+)^\sigma [\lambda] =  d_i B^i_\lambda,</math> therefore if we define the variations<math display="block">\delta_\lambda u^\sigma := (\mathcal{D}^+)^\sigma[\lambda]=\sum_{|I|=0}^s R^{\sigma,I}_a\lambda^a_I,</math>the variation<math display="block">\delta_\lambda L = E_\sigma \delta_\lambda u^\sigma + d_i W^i_\lambda
= d_i\left(B^i_\lambda + W^i_\lambda\right)</math>of the Lagrangian is a total divergence, hence the variations <math display="inline">\delta_\lambda u^\sigma</math> are quasi-symmetries for every value of the functions <math>\lambda^a</math>.
